extracted.intended_audience: communications and public relations (PR) professionals, marketers, and anyone writing press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guide for composing effective press releases that attract media attention and readership, covering structure, AP style, SEO, length, visuals, and distribution considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release structure / basic components
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-structured release makes your message easy to understand and easy to promote; basic components include headline, dateline, lead paragraph, body content, quote, provide data, call to action, boilerplate, media contact information, images/video or other multimedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the listed layout (headline; dateline; lead paragraph using five Ws; body content with supporting details and quotes; quote; provide data; call to action; boilerplate; media contact; images/video). All press releases tend to follow this layout, but go beyond simply following a template to make yours effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft a headline with no more than 100 characters that uses strong action verbs to answer the question: 'Why should I care?' and prompts your audience to continue reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the headline concise and specific; capitalise only the first word and proper nouns; use relevant keywords; be clear and direct (avoid ambiguous words/jargon); use strong action verbs (e.g., 'unveil', 'reveal' preferred over 'launch'); write in active voice; include numbers or data when possible. Note: elsewhere the page also suggests aiming for 70 characters or less in the FAQ — treat shorter headlines as preferable for some channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the city and date showing where and when the press release was issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP Style: Start the first paragraph with the city in ALL CAPS, followed by the state abbreviation and the date; well-known cities may omit the state abbreviation (example: 'LONDON, May 6, 2024').

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead paragraph (five Ws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a summary of the essential details in the first paragraph using the five Ws: who, what, when, where and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the most crucial information so journalists can quickly grasp the story; lead paragraph should summarise the core news and motivate reading the rest of the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body content and paragraphing
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand on the lead paragraph with supporting details and quotes. Keep paragraphs short, with one idea per paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short paragraphs for scannability; each paragraph should contain a single idea and support the main message introduced in the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a quote
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a quote from a relevant stakeholder or expert to add credibility and a human touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes should come from relevant stakeholders or experts and humanise the story; AP Style: use double quotation marks and introduce quotes with the speaker’s full name and title on first reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide data / back up claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Back up any claims with relevant statistics, survey results, historical context or industry trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your own data or reputable third-party sources to build trust and increase chances of pickup; include numbers or data in headline or body where appropriate to strengthen credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call to action
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a clear call to action to encourage readers to take the next step, like a link to a microsite or landing page for more details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align the call to action with the press release's goal (e.g., drive visits, registrations, downloads); place CTA clearly so journalists and readers can follow up easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a brief description of the organisation issuing the press release, highlighting its mission and expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the boilerplate concise and consistent across releases; it should succinctly convey the organisation’s identity and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide details for media inquiries, including names, emails and phone numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List specific contact names, email addresses, and phone numbers so journalists can quickly reach the right person for follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images, video or other multimedia
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding visual elements can increase engagement with your press release, especially if you add video or images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include high-quality images, videos or links to multimedia assets to improve pick-up and audience engagement; consider which visuals best support the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review press release examples
rubrics_metrics.description: It's a good idea to review successful examples of press releases as a starting point for crafting your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study press releases within your industry and ones that match your purpose (product launch, event, report) to learn structures, tone, and elements that performed well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding who your readers are is crucial. Are you addressing industry professionals, potential customers or a broader audience?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor message and language to the target audience; consider what aspects of the news will resonate and how the audience prefers to consume information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise / word count
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for a press release word count of 300 to 500 words to keep your message clear and focused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary jargon and stick to essential details. Use shorter (~300 words) releases for minor updates, time-sensitive news, or teasers; use longer releases for complex topics, research/reports, or major announcements that require added context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay relevant / timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell your audience why they should care; connect your story to current trends, industry developments or broader social issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A timely, relevant press release is more likely to be picked up; explicitly explain relevance and newsworthiness in headline and lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell a story / humanise
rubrics_metrics.description: Write your press release like a mini-story with a clear beginning, middle and end that weaves a compelling narrative and invites curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanise content by including quotes from someone directly affected by the story and structuring the release to build interest and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate SEO
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate relevant keywords, optimising headlines and descriptions and utilising backlinks to help your press release achieve higher visibility on SERPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SEO best practices: select relevant keywords, optimize title and meta/description where possible, and include backlinks to authoritative pages to increase discoverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide credibility through sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Support your message with statistics, research or industry reports, either your own or from another reputable source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite reputable sources and data to build trust with journalists and readers; include context or links to full reports when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and refine / editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Edit thoroughly for grammar, style and flow. Proofread to catch typos, grammar errors and awkward phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-read to ensure every word serves a purpose and the key message is conveyed; polishing increases professionalism and likelihood of pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP Style compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Associated Press (AP) Style, the widely used standard for journalism and press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key AP rules noted on the page: headline capitalise only first word and proper nouns; dateline formatting (city in ALL CAPS, state abbrev, date); numbers — spell out one to nine, use numerals for 10+ and always numerals for ages and percentages; dates — write month fully if alone or with year; abbreviate certain months when used with a date (Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec.); quotes — use double quotation marks and introduce quotes with speaker’s full name and title on first reference; titles — capitalise job titles only if they come before a name; acronyms — spell out on first use with abbreviation in parentheses; punctuation — use one space after a period and do not use the Oxford comma; overall structure — begin with the most crucial information (who, what, when, where, why) in the first paragraph, then follow with quotes and supporting information.
